label: University and jobs
rationale: Getting in somewhere: looking for work, finding it, entering a university or company, the experience you bring.
mixUps: Looking is shigoto o sagasu (o) but finding is shigoto ga mitsukaru (ga); daigaku and kaisha both take ni hairu, and keiken takes ga aru, not motsu.

targets.use: Said about job hunting, mostly in -teru: ima shigoto sagashiteru (I'm looking for work). Casual speech drops o.
targets.notes: Changing jobs is tenshoku suru; students' job hunting is shuukatsu.

example.romaji: ima atarashii shigoto sagashiteru n da.
example.ja: 今新しい仕事探してるんだ。
example.english: I'm looking for a new job right now.

examplePolite.romaji: ima atarashii shigoto o sagashiteru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今新しい仕事を探してるんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm looking for a new job right now.

targets.verbSense: be found, turn up (intransitive of mitsukeru)
targets.use: The usual way to share or ask job news, almost always in the past: atarashii shigoto mitsukatta? Casual speech drops ga, and mada mitsukaranai means you're still looking.
targets.notes: Both work: shigoto mitsuketa (I found one) and shigoto mitsukatta (one turned up); the question is usually mitsukatta? Congratulating: shigoto mitsukatte yokatta ne.

example.ja: やっと仕事見つかった！

examplePolite.ja: やっと仕事が見つかりました！

targets.verbSense: go in, enter; join (a school, company or club)
targets.trap: 'Start university' tempts daigaku o hajimeru. You enter a school: daigaku ni hairu (formally nyuugaku suru). Going there day to day is daigaku ni iku or kayou.
targets.use: Said in life stories, often as haitte kara (since I started) or haitta toki (when I started). Casual speech can drop ni; passing the entrance exam itself is daigaku ni ukaru.
targets.notes: Graduating is daigaku o deru or sotsugyou suru.

example.ja: 大学入ってから一人暮らししてる。
example.english: I've lived alone since I started university.

examplePolite.romaji: daigaku ni haitte kara hitorigurashi o shitemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 大学に入ってから一人暮らしをしてます。
examplePolite.english: I've lived alone since I started university.

targets.verbSense: go in, enter; join (a school, company or club)
targets.trap: 'Join a company' tempts sanka suru, which is taking part in an event. Joining a firm, school or club is hairu: kaisha ni haitta.
targets.use: Said in self-introductions and work history: kono kaisha ni haitte sannen (three years since I joined). Casual speech can drop ni; the formal word is nyuusha suru.
targets.notes: Leaving for good is kaisha o yameru; kaisha ni iku is just going to the office.

example.ja: この会社入って、もう三年。
example.english: It's been three years since I joined this company.

examplePolite.romaji: kono kaisha ni haitte, mou sannen desu.
examplePolite.ja: この会社に入って、もう三年です。
examplePolite.english: It's been three years since I joined this company.

targets.trap: 'Have experience' tempts keiken o motteru, which sounds like a CV. Experience exists: keiken aru? For one thing you've done once, -ta koto aru is more natural: itta koto aru?
partners: buranku (a gap in your work history: buranku ga aru)
targets.use: Said in job talk and about life, usually with what kind before it: baito no keiken aru? Casual speech drops ga, and the negative keiken nai (I've never done it) is common too.
targets.notes: After a trip or a hard time: ii keiken ni natta (it was a good experience).

example.romaji: kou iu shigoto no keiken aru?
example.ja: こういう仕事の経験ある？
example.english: Have you done this kind of work before?

examplePolite.romaji: kou iu shigoto no keiken wa arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: こういう仕事の経験はありますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you have experience with this kind of work?
